title: England Moved the Start Times. India's TV Audience Was the Reason.
excerpt: The ECB shifted three T20I matches by an hour to capture Indian viewers. All ODI tickets are sold. The financial report says the quiet part out loud.
body:
Three of the five T20I matches between England and India will now start at 5:30 PM local time instead of 6:30 PM. The change, confirmed last week after discussions between the England and Wales Cricket Board, Sky Sports, and Sony Sports Network, was made for one reason: to ensure the matches begin at 10 PM IST instead of 11 PM, catching Indian viewers before they switch off for the night.

It is a small adjustment. It is also a remarkably honest one.

## The Numbers Behind the Decision

The ECB's own financial report, published this year, states what cricket administrators rarely say in public: England cricket's revenues are "inherently cyclical, reflecting the scheduling of high-value broadcast series by opposition." The report projects a profit this year — the year India tours. It also projects losses in 2027, the year Australia tours for the Ashes.

Let that settle. The home of cricket expects to lose money hosting the Ashes. It expects to make money hosting India.

The arithmetic is straightforward. India's television market delivers hundreds of millions of viewers. An hour's shift in start time can mean the difference between a prime-time audience and a late-night one. Sony Sports Network, which holds Indian broadcast rights, was part of the discussions that led to the change. The remaining two T20Is will stay at 6:30 PM local time (11 PM IST).

## A Tour That Is Already a Sellout

Tickets for the tour went on sale late last year. All three ODIs — in Chester-le-Street, Manchester, and the Oval — have sold out. Only a few hundred seats remain across the five T20I venues. The demand is not hard to explain: Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli are expected to feature in the ODI series, and the T20I squad includes 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, whose IPL heroics have made him the most talked-about young cricketer on the planet.

The Ireland leg of the tour — two T20Is in Belfast on June 26 and 28 — has also sold out. An estimated 4,500 spectators per match at the Civil Service Ground in Stormont, most of them there to see Sooryavanshi's potential international debut.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs in the UK, this is a home series in everything but name. Indian fans have dominated English cricket crowds for years, turning venues into extensions of Indian stadiums. The ECB knows this. The rescheduled timings are an acknowledgement that the financial health of English cricket depends not just on English fans, but on a global Indian audience that spans time zones.

The five T20Is run from July 1 to July 11. The three ODIs follow from July 15 to July 19. During the peak of the English summer, sunset comes after 9 PM, so every match will finish under floodlights regardless of the start time.

For Indian fans in the UK, the earlier start also means matches end closer to 9 PM instead of 10 PM — easier on a weeknight. For fans in India, the difference between a 10 PM and 11 PM start is the difference between watching and sleeping. The ECB, it appears, has chosen watching.

## The Bigger Picture

India's upcoming schedule is relentless. The ODI series against Afghanistan begins on June 13 in Dharamsala. The team then travels to Belfast for two T20Is against Ireland, before crossing over to England for the main event. Simultaneously, the Women's T20 World Cup begins in England on June 12, and the FIFA World Cup kicks off in North America on June 11.

It is a month where Indian sports fans — at home and abroad — will have more live sport to watch than hours in the day. The ECB's decision to shift start times is a small concession to that reality. But it reveals a larger truth: in world cricket's financial ecosystem, India is not just the biggest market. It is the market.

The two remaining T20Is at their original 6:30 PM start will test whether the later slot loses viewers. If it does, expect next time around, every match will start earlier. The audience has spoken. The schedule is listening.
